notes.meaning: Ahithophel urged Absalom to strike quickly without giving David time to prepare. He volunteered to lead twelve thousand picked troops that very night to chase down the fleeing king. By moving with such speed, he hoped to crush David's cause before an army could gather around him.

Ahithophel planned to catch David while he was exhausted and vulnerable, sending his followers into a blind panic so they would scatter. His goal was to kill only David, sparing the rest of the nation and bringing the people smoothly under Absalom's rule. He argued that removing the king alone would end the rebellion quickly and restore peace without endless civil war.

Absalom and the leaders of Israel enthusiastically endorsed Ahithophel's plan. They were accustomed to treating his advice almost like the direct word of God. The cold-blooded plan to assassinate the king seemed the most practical path to securing the throne.

Even though everyone had approved Ahithophel's counsel, Absalom unexpectedly sent for Hushai to ask his opinion. Absalom explained Ahithophel's strategy and asked whether they should follow it or do something else. This surprising hesitation was God's unseen providence at work to rescue David.

Hushai boldly declared that, on this single occasion, Ahithophel's counsel was not wise. He was careful not to insult Ahithophel's overall reputation for wisdom, which made his objection sound honest and objective. This respectful opening gave Hushai the room he needed to introduce an entirely different plan.

Hushai reminded Absalom that David and his veteran soldiers were dangerous, battle-tested warriors who were now as furious as a mother bear robbed of her cubs. He pointed out that David was far too experienced in military tactics to sleep out in the open among the ordinary troops. Rushing into the dark after such desperate fighters would be an enormous risk.

Hushai warned that David was probably hidden away in a cave, waiting to spring an ambush on any small force sent after him. If Absalom's advance troops suffered even a minor defeat, rumors of a disaster would spread quickly and melt the courage of their best soldiers. Fear would spread easily because everyone in Israel knew how fiercely David's elite warriors could fight.

Instead of a quick strike, Hushai proposed raising a massive national army from one end of Israel to the other, as countless as the sand by the sea. He also flattered Absalom by insisting that the prince himself must march out and lead this vast force. Hushai's true aim was to buy David precious time to escape and gather his own loyal forces.

Hushai painted a vivid picture of total victory, claiming this massive army would fall upon David like thick dew blanketing the earth, leaving no survivors. Even if David fled behind the walls of a fortified city, the endless troops could bring ropes and pull the town down into the valley until not a pebble was left. These dramatic exaggerations appealed directly to Absalom's vanity and desire for a grand spectacle.

Absalom and his leaders were completely won over and judged Hushai's advice to be better than Ahithophel's. The sacred writer reveals that the Lord Himself caused this to happen, overturning Ahithophel's sound tactical plan in order to bring ruin upon Absalom. God showed His supreme control over human plans and answered David's earlier prayer for Ahithophel's counsel to be defeated.

Hushai immediately went to the loyal priests, Zadok and Abiathar, and explained what both he and Ahithophel had advised the council. He urged them to get an urgent warning to David not to camp near the river fords that night, but to cross the Jordan right away. Hushai knew Absalom was fickle and might still change his mind and send Ahithophel after the king.

The priests' sons, Jonathan and Ahimaaz, were stationed outside the city at the spring of En-rogel so they would not arouse suspicion by entering Jerusalem. A servant girl carried the secret message to them, likely pretending she was simply going out to draw water. The young men were prepared to run from there and deliver the warning straight to David.

A young boy spotted the messengers and reported them to Absalom, forcing Jonathan and Ahimaaz to run for their lives. They hurried into the village of Bahurim and hid inside a dry cistern in a loyal man's courtyard. The man's wife quickly spread a cloth over the well's opening and covered it with crushed grain, making it look like she was merely drying food in the sun.

When Absalom's search party arrived and questioned the woman, she misled them by claiming the men had already crossed over the water. The soldiers searched the area without finding them and eventually gave up the chase and went back to Jerusalem. God preserved the runners through this woman's quick thinking, even though she told a direct falsehood to protect them.

As soon as the pursuers were gone, the two young men climbed out of the cistern and ran to David, urging him to cross the river immediately. David and his followers obeyed without delay, traveling through the night to ford the Jordan. By daybreak, every single person with David had crossed safely, with not one soul left behind.

When Ahithophel realized his advice had been rejected, he saddled his donkey, went home, organized his household affairs, and hanged himself. He was driven by wounded pride at losing his influence, and he shrewdly foresaw that the rebellion was doomed and he would face execution as a traitor. He was buried in his family tomb, leaving behind a tragic portrait of worldly wisdom ruined by sinful choices.

David retreated to the fortified city of Mahanaim east of the Jordan, which gave him a safe base to regroup. Meanwhile, Absalom mobilized the national army as Hushai had suggested and led the Israelite forces across the river in pursuit. The delay in gathering these forces gave David the breathing room he needed to prepare for the clash.

Absalom appointed Amasa to lead his army in place of Joab, who had remained loyal to David. Amasa was closely related to David's family, being a cousin to Joab through their mothers. Absalom then moved his massive army into the region of Gilead and set up camp, preparing to fight his father.

When David arrived at Mahanaim, three wealthy and influential local leaders—Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai—came forward to support him. Recognizing that David's people were exhausted, hungry, and thirsty from their flight, they generously brought beds, cooking bowls, and large amounts of grains, honey, cheese, and livestock. God provided comfort and practical help through these generous allies just when David's own family had turned against him.
